title: Chien-Shiung Wu: The First Lady of Physics
summary: How the physicist Chien-Shiung Wu designed an extremely precise experiment that proved a long-trusted rule of physics, called parity, could be broken.
poll: The person who proves an idea with a careful experiment deserves as much credit as the person who first thought of the idea.

versions.title: The Scientist Who Found a Broken Rule
versions.text:
A girl named Wu was born in China. This was in 1912. She liked math. She grew up to be a scientist.

Wu moved to the U.S. She studied there. She ran a test. It used tiny bits called particles.

One day, two men had an idea. They thought a rule was wrong. The rule had a name: parity. It said things act the same both ways.

Wu knew how to test this. She used cold metal called cobalt. She made it very cold. She used a magnet. It lined up tiny bits in the metal.

Then she watched the bits fly out. The old rule said they should go out the same way. They did not! More went one way than the other.

This test proved the rule was wrong. The two men got a prize for it. Wu ran the test. She did not get the prize too.

Wu kept working for many years. People call her the First Lady of Physics.

A girl named Chien-Shiung Wu was born near Shanghai, China, in 1912. She loved math from a young age. She grew up to become a physicist, a scientist who studies tiny particles and the forces between them.

Wu moved to the U.S. to study, and later she became a respected professor. She worked very hard. She became known as one of the most careful scientists running an experiment with particles inside atoms.

One day, two other men had a bold idea. They thought an old, trusted rule of nature might not always be true. The rule was called parity. It said that nature should behave the same way, even as a mirror image.

Wu knew just how to test this idea. She used a metal called cobalt and cooled it to a very low temperature. Then she used a strong magnet, and it lined up all the atoms so they pointed one way.

Then she watched the tiny bits shoot out as the atoms broke apart. This is called beta decay. If the rule were true, the bits should fly out the same way on both sides. But they did not! Far more bits flew out one way than the other.

This test proved the old rule was broken, at least for this one kind of force. It was a huge discovery in physics. The two men who had the idea won a famous prize for it. But Wu, who had set up and run the test, did not share in the prize.

Wu kept doing work for many more years at a big school. People began calling her the First Lady of Physics because of her skill.

versions.title: Chien-Shiung Wu: Breaking a Rule of Nature
versions.text:
Chien-Shiung Wu was born near Shanghai, China, in 1912. She loved math from a young age. She grew up to become a physicist, a scientist who runs tests on tiny particles and the forces between them.

In 1936, Wu moved to the U.S. to keep studying. She earned a high degree and became a professor. Over the years, she became known as a careful scientist. She was skilled with particles inside the core, or nucleus, of an atom.

In 1956, two other men, Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang, had a bold theory. They thought a long-trusted rule of nature, called parity, might not always hold true. The rule said that nature should act the same way, even when seen as a mirror image, a kind of symmetry.

Lee and Yang needed an expert to test their idea. So they asked Wu to set up the test and confirm or disprove it. She picked a metal called cobalt-60, cooled it to a very low heat, and used a strong magnet. This lined up the cores of the atoms so they all pointed one way.

Then Wu carefully watched which way tiny bits called electrons shot out. This happened as the atoms broke apart, called beta decay. If parity held true, the bits should fly out the same on both sides. Instead, far more shot out in one direction than the other.

This showed that parity could be broken, at least for this one force, called the weak force. It was one of the great finds of modern physics. Lee and Yang won a famous prize for their idea. But Wu, who set up and ran the test that proved it, was left out of the prize.

Wu kept doing her work for many more decades at a big school. She later became the first woman to lead a large group of U.S. physicists. Today, people still call her the First Lady of Physics.

versions.title: Chien-Shiung Wu: The Experiment That Broke a Rule of Nature
versions.text:
Chien-Shiung Wu was born in 1912 near Shanghai, China, at a time when few girls were pushed toward science careers. She loved mathematics from a young age. She grew up to become a physicist known for designing precise experiments that probed subatomic particles and the forces between them.

In 1936, Wu moved to the United States to continue her studies. She earned a doctorate in physics at Berkeley, where she studied under leading nuclear physicists. She later began teaching at Columbia University. Over the following decades, she became known worldwide as a top expert in beta decay, a radioactive process in which an atom's nucleus gives off an electron.

In 1956, two physicists, Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang, proposed a bold and controversial idea that challenged decades of settled physics. They thought that parity conservation, a long-trusted rule, might not hold true for a fundamental force called the weak interaction. Parity conservation says nature should act the same whether seen directly or as a mirror image. The weak interaction is the force that governs beta decay.

Lee and Yang needed an experimenter skilled enough for this demanding task, so they turned to Wu, whose command of radioactive metals had no equal. She chose the isotope cobalt-60, cooled it near absolute zero, and applied a strong magnetic field so that the spins of its nuclei all pointed in one shared direction.

Wu then carefully measured which way electrons shot out from the cobalt nuclei during beta decay, comparing the count emitted each way. If parity held true, the electrons should have come out in equal numbers both ways. Instead, her careful count showed far more electrons emitted in one direction than the other, a sharp and striking asymmetry.

This result gave strong empirical proof that parity is violated within the weak interaction, overturning a rule physicists had trusted for decades without serious doubt. It became one of the most celebrated experiments in modern physics. Lee and Yang won the Nobel Prize the following year for their theoretical idea, yet Wu, who had designed and run the decisive test that proved it, was left out of the prize, a choice many physicists have since called unfair.

Wu kept doing groundbreaking research for several more decades at Columbia University, eventually becoming the first woman elected president of a national society of physicists. Historians of science still honor her lasting legacy as the First Lady of Physics.

Chien-Shiung Wu was born in 1912 near Shanghai, China. Few girls were pushed toward scientific careers then, let alone one as demanding as experimental physics. She developed a passion for mathematics from an early age. She matured into a physicist renowned for designing precise experiments. Her work probed subatomic particles and the forces acting between them.

In 1936, Wu traveled to the United States to continue her education. She earned a doctorate in physics at Berkeley. There she studied under leading nuclear physicists. She later became a respected professor at Columbia University. Over the following decades, she gained recognition as one of the most accomplished experimentalists working with beta decay. This is a radioactive process in which a nucleus emits an electron.

In 1956, two theoretical physicists, Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang, proposed a bold and controversial idea. It challenged decades of settled physics. They suspected that parity conservation, a long-trusted principle, might not hold true for a fundamental force called the weak interaction. Parity conservation assumes that nature behaves identically when observed as a mirror image. The weak interaction is the force responsible for beta decay.

Lee and Yang required an experimenter skilled enough to test their hypothesis under demanding conditions. So they approached Wu, whose command of radioactive materials had no equal among her peers. She selected the isotope cobalt-60. She cooled it to a fraction of a degree above absolute zero. Then she applied a powerful magnetic field so that the spins of its nuclei aligned in a single shared direction.

Wu then measured the direction in which electrons were ejected from the cobalt nuclei during beta decay, comparing the number emitted each way. If parity conservation held true, the electrons should have been emitted in equal numbers in both directions. Instead, her measurements revealed substantially more electrons emitted one way than the other, an unmistakable asymmetry.

This result gave clear empirical proof that parity is violated within the weak interaction. It overturned an assumption physicists had accepted for decades without serious challenge. It stands today as one of the most celebrated experiments in twentieth-century physics. Lee and Yang received the Nobel Prize the following year for their theoretical prediction. Yet Wu, who had designed and performed the decisive experiment that proved it, was controversially excluded from the award, a decision many physicists have since criticized as unjust.

Wu continued conducting groundbreaking research for several more decades at Columbia University, eventually becoming the first woman elected president of the American Physical Society. Historians of science continue to honor her legacy as the First Lady of Physics, a title reflecting both her brilliance and her perseverance.

Chien-Shiung Wu was born in 1912 near Shanghai, China. Few girls were encouraged to pursue scientific careers then, let alone one as demanding and technically exacting as experimental nuclear physics. Her work probed subatomic particles and the fundamental forces governing their interactions.

In 1936, Wu traveled to the United States to continue her education. She earned a doctorate in physics at Berkeley, where she studied under leading nuclear physicists, before becoming a respected professor at Columbia University. Over the following decades, she gained widespread recognition as one of the most meticulous and accomplished experimentalists working with beta decay. This is a radioactive process in which a nucleus emits an electron as it transforms into a different element.

In 1956, two theoretical physicists, Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang, proposed a bold and highly controversial idea that directly challenged decades of settled physical theory. They suspected that parity conservation, a long-trusted principle, might not hold true for a fundamental force called the weak interaction, the very force responsible for beta decay. So they approached Wu, whose command of radioactive materials and cryogenic, low-temperature techniques had no equal among her contemporaries. She selected the isotope cobalt-60. She cooled it to a tiny fraction of a degree above absolute zero. Then she applied a powerful magnetic field so that the nuclei aligned, their spins pointing in a single shared direction.

Instead, her painstaking measurements revealed substantially more electrons emitted in one direction than the other, an asymmetry that no previous experiment had ever observed.

This result gave clear empirical proof that parity is violated within the weak interaction. It overturned an assumption that physicists had accepted for decades without serious challenge. It stands today as one of the most celebrated and consequential experiments in twentieth-century physics. Lee and Yang received the Nobel Prize in Physics the following year for their theoretical prediction. Yet Wu, who had designed and performed the decisive experiment that actually proved it correct, was controversially excluded from the award, a decision many physicists have since openly criticized as a profound and lasting injustice.

Wu continued conducting groundbreaking research for several more decades at Columbia University, eventually becoming the first woman ever elected president of the American Physical Society. Historians of science continue to honor her enduring legacy as the First Lady of Physics, a title reflecting both her extraordinary brilliance and her remarkable, lifelong perseverance.

versions.title: Chien-Shiung Wu: The Experiment That Overturned a Fundamental Law of Nature
versions.text:
In 1912, in a small village near Shanghai, China, a girl was born who would grow into one of the twentieth century's most meticulous experimental physicists, at a time when few girls were encouraged to pursue scientific careers, let alone one as technically exacting as experimental nuclear physics. Chien-Shiung Wu cultivated a passion for mathematics from an early age, and she eventually matured into a scientist renowned internationally for designing extraordinarily precise experiments capable of probing the subtle behavior of subatomic particles and the fundamental forces governing their interactions.

In 1936, Wu traveled to the United States to continue her education, ultimately earning a doctorate in physics at the University of California, Berkeley, where she trained under leading nuclear physicists before eventually becoming a respected professor at Columbia University. Across the following decades, she gained widespread international recognition as among the most meticulous and accomplished experimentalists working with beta decay, a radioactive process in which an atomic nucleus spontaneously emits an electron as it transforms into a different element entirely.

In 1956, two theoretical physicists, Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang, proposed an audacious and highly controversial idea that directly challenged decades of settled physical theory. They suspected that a long-trusted principle known as parity conservation, the deeply entrenched assumption that nature behaves identically whether observed directly or through a mirror, might not hold true for a fundamental force called the weak interaction, the very force responsible for beta decay.

Lee and Yang required an experimenter skilled enough to test their controversial hypothesis under extraordinarily demanding laboratory conditions, and so they approached Wu, whose command of radioactive materials and cryogenic, extremely-low-temperature techniques was considered unrivaled among her contemporaries anywhere in the world. She selected the radioactive isotope cobalt-60, cooled it to a temperature only a minuscule fraction of a degree above absolute zero, and applied a powerful magnetic field so that the nuclei of its atoms aligned uniformly, their spins all pointing consistently in a single shared direction throughout the entire sample.

Wu then meticulously measured the direction in which electrons were ejected from the cobalt nuclei during beta decay, painstakingly comparing the number emitted along the spin direction with the number emitted against it. If parity conservation held true, the electrons should have been emitted in exactly equal numbers in both directions, exhibiting absolutely no preference for either. Instead, her measurements revealed substantially more electrons emitted in one direction than the other, an unmistakable and startling asymmetry that no previous experiment had ever managed to observe.

The profound significance of this finding lay in how decisively it settled a question that theorists alone could never have resolved through abstract reasoning or calculation alone; only a flawlessly executed empirical experiment, conducted at the very edge of what the equipment of the era could achieve, could demonstrate that a cherished and seemingly self-evident assumption about the underlying symmetry of nature was, in fact, simply false.

This landmark result demonstrated conclusively that parity is violated within the weak interaction, overturning an assumption that physicists had accepted for decades without serious challenge from any quarter whatsoever. It stands today as one of the most celebrated and consequential experiments in the entire history of twentieth-century physics. Lee and Yang received the Nobel Prize in Physics the following year for their theoretical prediction, yet Wu, who had personally designed and performed the decisive experiment that actually proved it correct, was controversially excluded from the award altogether, a decision many physicists and historians have since openly criticized as a profound and lasting injustice.

Wu continued conducting groundbreaking research for several more decades at Columbia University, eventually becoming the first woman ever elected president of the American Physical Society. Historians of science continue to honor her enduring legacy as the First Lady of Physics, a title reflecting both her extraordinary scientific brilliance and her remarkable, lifelong perseverance in a field that offered her few allies.

versions.title: Chien-Shiung Wu: The Experiment That Overturned a Fundamental Law of Nature
versions.text:
Born in 1912 within a small village near Shanghai, China, Chien-Shiung Wu would mature into one of the twentieth century's most meticulous and methodologically rigorous experimental physicists, at a historical moment when few girls were encouraged to pursue scientific careers, let alone one as technically exacting and mathematically demanding as experimental nuclear physics. From an early age, she cultivated an unmistakable passion for mathematics, ultimately developing into a scientist renowned internationally for designing extraordinarily precise experiments capable of probing the exceedingly subtle behavior of subatomic particles and the fundamental forces governing their myriad interactions.

In 1936, Wu traveled to the United States to continue her education, eventually earning a doctorate in physics at the University of California, Berkeley, where she trained extensively under preeminent nuclear physicists before ultimately becoming a distinguished professor at Columbia University. Across the ensuing decades, she garnered widespread international recognition as among the most meticulous and accomplished experimentalists specializing in beta decay, a radioactive process whereby an atomic nucleus spontaneously emits an electron as it transforms into an entirely different chemical element.

In 1956, two theoretical physicists, Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang, formulated an audacious and intensely controversial hypothesis that directly challenged decades of settled physical theory. They suspected that a long-trusted principle known as parity conservation, the deeply entrenched assumption that nature behaves identically whether observed directly or through its mirror reflection, might fail to hold true for a fundamental force designated the weak interaction, the very force responsible for beta decay.

Lee and Yang required an experimenter sufficiently skilled to test their controversial hypothesis under extraordinarily demanding laboratory conditions, and consequently they approached Wu, whose mastery of radioactive materials and cryogenic, extremely-low-temperature techniques was considered unrivaled among her contemporaries worldwide. She selected the radioactive isotope cobalt-60, cooled it to a temperature constituting only a minuscule fraction of a degree above absolute zero, and applied a formidable magnetic field so that the nuclei of its constituent atoms aligned uniformly, their intrinsic spins pointing consistently in a single shared orientation throughout the entirety of the sample.

Wu subsequently measured, with exacting precision, the direction in which electrons were ejected from the cobalt nuclei during beta decay, painstakingly comparing the quantity emitted along the spin direction against the quantity emitted in opposition to it. Had parity conservation held true, the electrons would have been emitted in precisely equal numbers in both directions, exhibiting absolutely no directional preference whatsoever. Instead, her measurements revealed substantially more electrons emitted in one direction than the other, an unmistakable and genuinely startling asymmetry that no previous experiment had ever succeeded in observing.

The profound significance of this finding resided in how decisively it resolved a question that theoretical reasoning alone could never have settled; only a flawlessly executed empirical experiment, conducted at the absolute limits of what contemporaneous equipment could achieve, could conclusively demonstrate that a cherished and seemingly self-evident assumption regarding the underlying symmetry of nature was, in actuality, fundamentally false.

This landmark result established conclusively that parity is violated within the weak interaction, thereby overturning an assumption that physicists had accepted unchallenged for decades. It endures today as one of the most celebrated and consequential experiments in the entire annals of twentieth-century physics. Lee and Yang subsequently received the Nobel Prize in Physics the following year in recognition of their theoretical prediction, yet Wu, who had personally designed and executed the decisive experiment that actually substantiated it, was controversially excluded from the award altogether, a decision that numerous physicists and historians have since openly condemned as a profound and enduring injustice.

Wu continued conducting groundbreaking research for several further decades at Columbia University, eventually becoming the first woman ever elected president of the American Physical Society. Historians of science continue to commemorate her enduring legacy as the First Lady of Physics, a title reflecting both her extraordinary scientific brilliance and her remarkable, lifelong perseverance within a field that afforded her remarkably few allies.

questions.why: The article shows that without Wu's careful experiment, the idea would never have been proven, so many felt she deserved credit too.

wrong.C: She worked extremely hard and carefully on the experiment.
wrong.D: The two men needed her skill to test their idea.

questions.stem: What can you tell about Wu from how she kept working for many years?
options: She gave up easily when things got hard.
She was determined and loved her work.
She only liked easy, simple tasks.
She never wanted to be a scientist.
questions.why: Continuing important research for many years shows that Wu was dedicated and passionate about her work.

wrong.A: She faced a very hard, difficult experiment and succeeded.
wrong.C: Her experiment was extremely difficult, not simple.
wrong.D: She clearly loved science and became a scientist.

questions.stem: Why do people call Wu the First Lady of Physics?
options: She ruled a country as a queen.
She was the only woman ever to study science.
People wanted to honor her great work in physics.
She built the first magnet ever made.
questions.why: Giving someone a special title is a way of honoring their important work, and Wu's experiment was a huge discovery.

wrong.A: She was a scientist, not a ruler.
wrong.B: The article does not say she was the only woman in science.
wrong.D: Magnets already existed long before Wu used one.

questions.stem: Read this sentence: "It said nature acts the same way, like in a mirror." What is this sentence describing?
options: A tool used to measure particles
The place where Wu was born
The rule called parity
The prize that two men won
questions.why: The article uses this sentence to explain what the rule called parity means.

wrong.A: A magnet is the tool, not described this way.
wrong.B: Her birthplace is not described as a mirror.
wrong.D: The prize is a different idea from the rule itself.

LOW.prompt: Explain the steps Wu used to test whether the rule about parity was true. Use the words first, next, and then.
checklist: I told all three steps in order.
I used the words first, next, and then.
I used facts from the article.
LOW.modelAnswer: First, Wu cooled a metal called cobalt to a very low temperature and used a magnet to line up its atoms. Next, she watched the tiny particles shoot out of the atoms as they broke apart. Then she compared how many particles flew out in each direction and found that more went one way, proving the old rule was wrong.

keyWords.definition: a scientist who studies matter, energy, and the forces of the universe
keyWords.example: The physicist explained why the bridge needed strong steel cables.

keyWords.definition: having to do with the center, or nucleus, of an atom
keyWords.example: A nuclear power plant uses energy from inside atoms to make electricity.

keyWords.definition: a carefully reasoned explanation of how or why something happens, based on evidence
keyWords.example: Scientists tested their theory about the storm by checking weather records.

keyWords.definition: when two sides or parts of something match each other exactly
keyWords.example: The butterfly's wings showed perfect symmetry, with matching spots on each side.

keyWords.definition: to show that something is true using evidence or a test
keyWords.example: A second test helped confirm that the water really was safe to drink.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?
options: Wu designed a precise experiment that proved a rule called parity could be broken.
Wu was the first person from China to study in the United States.
Lee and Yang discovered cobalt-60 while studying ordinary chemistry in school.
The weak interaction between particles was first observed using a giant telescope.
questions.why: The article focuses on how Wu's careful experiment with cobalt-60 proved that parity is violated in the weak interaction.

wrong.B: Being the first Chinese student in the United States is not stated or the main idea.
wrong.C: Cobalt-60 was not discovered by Lee and Yang; it was chosen as a tool for the experiment.
wrong.D: A telescope is not mentioned; her tools were cobalt, cold temperatures, and a magnet.

questions.stem: What did the rule called parity claim about nature?
options: That nature behaves the same way viewed directly or as a mirror image
That all metals conduct electricity equally well
That cold temperatures always slow down moving particles quite a lot indeed
That magnets always attract every single type of metal and material equally
questions.why: The article explains that parity said nature should behave identically when viewed as a mirror image.

wrong.B: Electrical conductivity of metals is not discussed.
wrong.C: Cold temperature was part of her method, not the content of the rule.
wrong.D: Magnet attraction to metals is not what parity claims.

questions.stem: What radioactive material did Wu use in her experiment?
options: Gold
Cobalt-60
Silver
Uranium ore
questions.why: The article states that Wu selected the radioactive metal cobalt-60 for her experiment.

wrong.A: Gold is not mentioned in the article.
wrong.C: Silver is not mentioned in the article.
wrong.D: Uranium ore is not part of this particular experiment.

questions.stem: Why did Wu cool the cobalt to such an extremely low temperature?
options: So the magnet could line up the nuclei of the atoms clearly
So the cobalt would turn into a liquid
So the particles would move faster than usual
So the cobalt would stop being radioactive
questions.why: Cooling the cobalt to near absolute zero let the magnetic field line up the atoms' nuclei so their spins pointed the same way, which the experiment needed.

wrong.B: The article does not say the cobalt became liquid.
wrong.C: Extreme cold is used to reduce random motion, not speed particles up for this purpose.
wrong.D: The cobalt stayed radioactive; that was necessary for beta decay to happen.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from the fact that far more electrons flew out in one direction than the other?
options: The old rule about parity was correct after all.
The magnet in the experiment was broken.
Nature does not always behave the same as its mirror image.
The cobalt had not been cooled enough.
questions.why: An uneven result is exactly what parity predicted should not happen, showing that nature's behavior is not always symmetric like a mirror image.

wrong.A: An uneven result contradicts, rather than supports, the old rule.
wrong.B: The article presents the magnet as working correctly for the experiment.
wrong.D: The article presents the cooling as successful and necessary for the result.

questions.stem: What can the reader infer about why Lee and Yang needed Wu specifically?
options: She was the only physicist who liked cold temperatures.
Her exceptional skill with careful experiments made her the right person to test their idea.
She had already won the Nobel Prize before this experiment.
She happened to live closest to their laboratory.
questions.why: The article describes Wu as known for being extremely careful and skilled at experiments, which is why two theorists turned to her to test their idea.

wrong.A: Liking cold temperatures is not given as a reason.
wrong.C: She had not yet won the prize; in fact, she never received it for this work.
wrong.D: Location is not mentioned as a reason she was chosen.

questions.stem: In the article, confirm most nearly means —
options: to guess without any evidence
to show something is true using a test
to completely ignore an idea
to disagree loudly with someone
questions.why: Wu's experiment confirmed, or showed with evidence, that parity could be broken.

wrong.A: Confirming involves evidence, not a random guess.
wrong.C: Confirming means paying close attention to an idea, not ignoring it.
wrong.D: Confirming is about proof, not disagreement.

questions.stem: How does the author mainly organize the explanation of Wu's discovery?
options: By listing every prize she ever won
By comparing the old rule with what her experiment actually showed
By describing many different scientists from different countries
By explaining how cobalt is used in jewelry
questions.why: The article repeatedly contrasts what parity predicted with what Wu's experiment actually found, building toward the discovery.

wrong.A: Only one prize, the Nobel Prize, is discussed.
wrong.C: The article focuses mainly on Wu, Lee, and Yang.
wrong.D: Jewelry is not mentioned.

MID.prompt: Compare what the rule of parity predicted with what Wu's experiment actually showed. Explain why this made her experiment so important, using details from the article.
checklist: I described what the experiment actually showed.
I explained why this made the experiment important, using details from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: The rule of parity predicted that electrons should fly out equally in both directions when the cobalt atoms decayed, since nature was assumed to behave the same way as its mirror image. However, Wu's experiment actually showed that far more electrons flew out in one direction than the other. This made her experiment extremely important because it proved, with real evidence, that parity could be broken for the weak interaction, overturning an assumption that physicists had trusted for decades.

keyWords.definition: the physics principle that a system should behave the same way whether observed directly or as its mirror image
keyWords.example: The engineer joked that the twin machines showed perfect parity, running in perfect mirror-image motion.

keyWords.definition: smaller than an atom, such as a particle inside an atom's nucleus
keyWords.example: A powerful accelerator smashes subatomic particles together at incredible speeds.

keyWords.definition: in physics, the principle that a certain quantity stays the same during a process
keyWords.example: The conservation of energy means energy cannot simply disappear in a closed system.

keyWords.definition: based on evidence from observation or experiment rather than theory alone
keyWords.example: The committee wanted empirical proof, not just a clever argument, before approving the new medicine.

keyWords.definition: a lack of balance or equality between two sides of something
keyWords.example: The architect noticed a slight asymmetry between the two towers of the bridge.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Wu's rigorous experiment provided the empirical proof that overturned the assumption of parity conservation in the weak interaction.
Lee and Yang personally performed the cobalt-60 experiment in their own laboratory.
Parity conservation has never been questioned by any physicist since Wu's experiment.
Cobalt-60 was invented by physicists specifically for Wu's research.
questions.why: The article centers on how Wu's carefully designed and executed experiment supplied the real-world evidence that disproved parity conservation for the weak interaction.

wrong.B: Lee and Yang proposed the theory; Wu designed and performed the experiment.
wrong.C: The article presents this as a settled, overturned assumption, not an ongoing debate.
wrong.D: Cobalt-60 is a naturally studied isotope, not something invented for this purpose.

questions.stem: According to the article, what did parity conservation assume about nature?
options: That nature behaves identically whether observed directly or as a mirror image
That radioactive materials decay at a constant, unchanging rate always
That magnetic fields cannot affect the nuclei of atoms
That electrons always travel faster than protons
questions.why: The article defines parity conservation as the assumption that nature behaves identically whether observed directly or as its mirror image.

wrong.B: Decay rate consistency is a different physical idea, not discussed here.
wrong.C: The experiment relies on a magnetic field successfully affecting the nuclei.
wrong.D: Relative speeds of electrons and protons are not discussed.

questions.stem: What specific technique allowed Wu to align the spins of the cobalt-60 nuclei?
options: Heating the sample to a very high temperature
Spinning the sample rapidly in a centrifuge
Cooling it near absolute zero and applying a strong magnetic field
Exposing the sample to very intense visible light for several hours
questions.why: The article explains that Wu cooled the cobalt-60 to a temperature just above absolute zero and applied a powerful magnetic field to align the nuclear spins.

wrong.A: Heating is the opposite of what the article describes.
wrong.B: A centrifuge is not mentioned in the article.
wrong.D: Visible light is not described as part of the method.

questions.stem: Why did the observed asymmetry in electron emission matter so much scientifically?
options: Because it contradicted what parity conservation predicted should happen
Because it proved cobalt-60 was not actually radioactive
Because it showed magnets have no effect on electrons
Because it confirmed that the Nobel Prize should go to Wu alone
questions.why: Parity conservation predicted equal emission in both directions, so the observed asymmetry directly contradicted and disproved that assumption.

wrong.B: The asymmetry depended on cobalt-60 actually undergoing beta decay.
wrong.C: The magnet's effect on alignment was essential to the experiment working at all.
wrong.D: The article does not frame the result as deciding who should receive the prize.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about why theoretical reasoning alone could not resolve the parity question?
options: Because Lee and Yang refused to explain their idea to anyone
Because only an empirical experiment could reveal how nature actually behaves
Because mathematics is never useful in physics
Because the question had already been answered centuries earlier
questions.why: The article states that only a flawlessly executed empirical experiment could demonstrate that the assumption about nature's symmetry was false, since reasoning alone cannot substitute for observation.

wrong.A: The article does not suggest they withheld their idea.
wrong.C: Mathematics is treated as essential to physics throughout the article.
wrong.D: The question was unresolved until Wu's 1956 experiment.

questions.stem: Why does the author emphasize that Wu was excluded from the Nobel Prize despite performing the decisive experiment?
options: To argue that experimental work is less important than theoretical work
To highlight an injustice and credit her essential contribution to the discovery
To suggest that Lee and Yang did not deserve any recognition
To prove that Wu never wanted scientific recognition at all
questions.why: The article points out that many physicists have criticized her exclusion, emphasizing how essential her experimental work was to proving the theory.

wrong.A: The article's framing suggests the opposite, since her experiment was decisive.
wrong.C: The article does not question Lee and Yang's theoretical contribution.
wrong.D: The article's tone suggests this exclusion was unfair, implying she deserved recognition.

questions.stem: In the article, the word empirical most nearly means —
options: based on evidence from observation or experiment
based purely on guesswork with no testing
related only to mathematics and equations
impossible to measure or observe directly
questions.why: The article uses empirical to describe an experiment grounded in real observation, in contrast to theory or reasoning alone.

wrong.B: Empirical is the opposite of mere guesswork.
wrong.C: Empirical refers to observation and experiment, not equations alone.
wrong.D: Empirical results come from things that can be measured.

questions.stem: How does Wu's approach differ from that of Lee and Yang?
options: Both scientists performed the exact same laboratory experiment.
Lee and Yang proposed the theoretical idea; Wu designed and executed the experimental test of it.
Wu proposed the theory, while Lee and Yang built the laboratory equipment.
Neither scientist contributed anything to the final discovery.
questions.why: Lee and Yang developed the theoretical hypothesis that parity might be violated, while Wu designed and carried out the precise experiment that tested and confirmed it.

wrong.A: Only Wu performed the laboratory experiment described in the article.
wrong.C: It is the reverse: Lee and Yang proposed the theory, and Wu built and ran the experiment.
wrong.D: Both made essential, distinct contributions to the discovery.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how Wu's experiment shows that scientific theories must be tested with empirical evidence before they can be trusted, using at least two details from the article.
checklist: I explained the relationship between theory and empirical evidence in my own words.
I connected this idea to at least two parts of Wu's experiment.
I supported my ideas with evidence from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Wu's experiment demonstrates that even a widely trusted scientific theory must be confirmed through empirical evidence before it can truly be accepted. Lee and Yang's theoretical idea that parity might be violated remained only a hypothesis until Wu carefully cooled cobalt-60 to near absolute zero and used a magnetic field to align its nuclei. When she measured a clear asymmetry in how electrons were emitted, this empirical result, not theoretical reasoning alone, proved that nature does not always behave symmetrically. This shows that in physics, careful observation and experimentation are what ultimately determine whether an idea is actually true.
